job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Superintelligence Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
For our explainer ahead of next Thursday's markup, we want to cover the bill's weak spots. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Superintelligence Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Superintelligence Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COVERED AI SYSTEM.—The term "covered AI system" means—
  (A) an artificial intelligence model trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations in a single training run; or
  (B) any artificial intelligence system that the Secretary determines is capable of substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks.
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED FACILITY.—The term "covered facility" means a data center containing more than 50,000 advanced AI chips.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to train, develop, or deploy a covered AI system.
(b) EXISTING SYSTEMS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to a covered AI system whose training began before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) SAFETY EVALUATION.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of safety evaluation.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered facility shall register the facility with the Department of Commerce.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the Department of Commerce a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the computing workloads run at the facility.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that covered AI systems can be developed safely.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
1. **Sec. 2(1) — “artificial intelligence model” and “artificial intelligence system” are undefined.** The bill uses the terms differently without explaining when software becomes a model or a system, allowing firms to characterize a product, ensemble, agent, or service as falling outside the covered category.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — The computation threshold lacks a measurement standard.** The text does not say whether to count attempted, completed, useful, estimated, theoretical, or hardware-level operations, nor who must calculate them, making the \(10^{26}\) threshold difficult to verify consistently.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — Exactly \(10^{26}\) operations are excluded.** Because coverage requires a quantity “greater than” \(10^{26}\), a run at precisely that threshold is not covered.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — “Single training run” invites segmentation.** A developer could divide training among successive runs, fine-tuning stages, separate model components, or cooperating entities and argue that no individual run crossed the threshold.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — Distributed and ensemble systems are not addressed.** Companies could train multiple sub-threshold models and combine them into an ensemble, mixture-of-experts system, or agent network whose aggregate capability exceeds that of a single covered model.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — The bill focuses on training compute, not inference compute.** Systems that achieve advanced capabilities through extensive test-time computation, retrieval, tools, or repeated model calls might remain outside the numerical definition.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — The fixed threshold can become obsolete.** The bill provides no mechanism to adjust \(10^{26}\) operations for algorithmic advances, new hardware, or improved measurement methods, so increasingly capable systems might be trained below it.

8. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — “The Secretary” is not identified.** Elsewhere the bill expressly refers to the Secretary of State, while the registry involves Commerce; this leaves unclear which Secretary makes capability determinations.

9. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — The capability test is highly indeterminate.** “Substantially exceeding human performance,” “most,” and “cognitive tasks” have no benchmarks, reference population, evaluation protocol, or specified treatment of uneven performance.

10. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — Coverage may depend on a prior agency determination.** The wording covers a system “that the Secretary determines” has the requisite capability, potentially allowing deployment until a system-specific determination is made and raising questions about notice, procedure, and judicial review.

11. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — The delegation has no standards or process.** The bill provides no deadlines, evidentiary requirements, rulemaking procedure, appeal mechanism, or limiting principles for the Secretary’s determinations, making them vulnerable to procedural, vagueness, or delegation challenges.

12. **Sec. 2(2) — The definition of “U.S. person” omits many people and entities.** It does not include permanent residents, partnerships, unincorporated associations, federally or territorially organized entities, or foreign entities controlled by Americans; “State” is also not defined to clearly include the District of Columbia and territories.

13. **Sec. 2(2) — Foreign subsidiaries present an evasion route.** A U.S. corporation could conduct work through a separately incorporated foreign subsidiary that is not itself a “corporation organized under the laws of a State,” subject to ordinary rules about attribution and control.

14. **Sec. 2(3) — “Advanced AI chips” is undefined.** Without performance, bandwidth, interconnect, age, or end-use criteria, operators cannot reliably determine which chips count and regulators could face serious classification disputes.

15. **Sec. 2(3) — Exactly 50,000 chips are excluded.** A facility “containing more than 50,000” covered chips can remain outside the registry at 50,000.

16. **Sec. 2(3) — Facilities can be divided or distributed.** Operators could split chips among neighboring buildings, campuses, corporate entities, or interconnected data centers and argue that no individual “data center” exceeds the threshold.

17. **Sec. 2(3) — “Data center,” “facility,” “containing,” and “operator” are undefined.** These omissions create uncertainty for leased chips, cloud customers, colocation sites, temporarily installed hardware, and facilities with multiple owners or operators.

18. **Sec. 3(a) — The operative verbs are undefined.** “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” could cover anything from basic research to commercial operation, yet leave disputes over fine-tuning, testing, copying, hosting, publishing model weights, providing an API, or integrating another company’s model.

19. **Sec. 3(a) — “Develop” may be unconstitutionally or impractically broad.** It could reach preliminary research, software tools, papers, or code that never produces a covered system; where publication or source code is involved, the breadth may also invite First Amendment challenges.

20. **Sec. 3(a) — Domestic territorial scope is unclear for networked activity.** The bill does not say where cloud-based or distributed training occurs when users, developers, servers, and corporate decision-makers are in different countries.

21. **Sec. 3(a) — Extraterritorial application is incomplete and contestable.** It reaches U.S. persons abroad but does not clearly cover their foreign subsidiaries, foreign contractors, or non-U.S. collaborators, and it supplies no special enforcement or service mechanisms for overseas conduct.

22. **Sec. 3(b) — The grandfather clause is exceptionally broad.** Once a covered system’s “training began” before enactment, the text appears to exempt not only that training but also later development and deployment indefinitely.

23. **Sec. 3(b) — “Training began” is undefined and easy to manipulate.** A company could conduct a token pre-enactment training step and claim that a much larger post-enactment effort is the same grandfathered training process.

24. **Sec. 3(b) — Materially changed systems may remain grandfathered.** The bill does not specify when fine-tuning, retraining, adding tools, expanding an architecture, or replacing data creates a new system rather than continuing an exempt one.

25. **Sec. 3(c) — The safety-evaluation exception has no guardrails.** “For the purpose of safety evaluation” requires no approval, protocol, compute limit, duration, containment, reporting, or independent oversight, allowing a developer to characterize ordinary capability work as safety testing.

26. **Sec. 3(c) — Mixed-purpose activity is unresolved.** The bill does not say whether safety must be the sole, primary, or merely one purpose, so an activity with commercial or capability-development objectives could potentially claim the exception.

27. **Sec. 3(c) — The exception appears to permit deployment.** Because it exempts “activities” from all of subsection (a), a company could argue that deployment to users, contractors, or researchers is part of a safety evaluation.

28. **Sec. 4 — The registry is poorly matched to the prohibition.** Registration applies only to facilities above the chip threshold, although prohibited systems could be trained across smaller facilities, on foreign infrastructure, or at lower compute under the capability-based definition.

29. **Sec. 4(a) — The registry’s geographic reach is missing.** “Each covered facility” literally contains no U.S. nexus, potentially purporting to regulate foreign facilities with no connection to the United States while leaving enforcement authority unclear.

30. **Sec. 4(a) — Registration procedures are absent.** There is no registration deadline, required information, updating obligation, change-of-control rule, or authority directing Commerce to issue implementing regulations.

31. **Sec. 4(b) — “Describing the computing workloads” is too vague.** The bill supplies no reporting fields, level of detail, compute-accounting method, records-retention period, submission deadline within each quarter, or treatment of customer confidentiality.

32. **Sec. 4(b) — Self-certification lacks verification mechanisms.** Commerce receives no express inspection, audit, subpoena, testing, or chip-tracking authority, making inaccurate workload reports difficult to detect.

33. **Secs. 4 and 5 — Registry violations carry no stated penalty.** Section 5 penalizes violations of section 3 only, so failure to register, report, or report accurately is not expressly subject to either listed penalty.

34. **Sec. 5 — The bill does not designate an enforcer or enforcement process.** It does not say which agency or official may bring civil actions, assess administrative penalties, seek injunctions, issue subpoenas, obtain warrants, or promulgate enforcement rules.

35. **Sec. 5(a) — Civil liability has no express knowledge requirement.** Strict liability may penalize actors who could not reasonably know a model’s compute history or capability status, strengthening fair-notice and due-process objections.

36. **Sec. 5(a) — The per-day formula does not fit every prohibited act.** Training and deployment may be continuous, intermittent, or instantaneous, and the bill does not explain when a violation begins, ends, or constitutes a separate daily violation.

37. **Sec. 5(a) — The maximum penalty may be treated as a cost of doing business.** “Not more than” $1 million supplies neither a minimum nor factors tied to company size, revenue, compute used, culpability, or economic benefit.

38. **Sec. 5(b) — “Willfully” is unexplained.** Courts could disagree whether prosecutors must prove only intentional conduct, knowledge of the relevant facts, or knowledge that the conduct was unlawful, creating uncertainty in criminal cases.

39. **Sec. 5 — Attempts, assistance, and evasive arrangements are not expressly covered.** The text does not specifically address attempted violations, financing, brokering, providing compute, directing foreign affiliates, or aiding and abetting, although some general federal criminal doctrines might apply.

40. **Secs. 5(a) and 8 — The penalty and effective-date provisions conflict.** Section 5 refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, while section 8 says the Act takes effect 180 days later; the better reading may be that no violation is possible before then, but the mismatch creates avoidable uncertainty.

41. **Sec. 6 — The international provision requires only an effort to negotiate.** The Secretary of State need only “seek” an agreement, with no requirement to conclude, submit, implement, or enforce one and no consequence if negotiations fail.

42. **Sec. 6 — “Equivalent” prohibitions are undefined.** Countries could disagree over whether different thresholds, exceptions, penalties, or enforcement arrangements are equivalent, weakening the provision’s practical value.

43. **Sec. 7(a) — The National Academies report has no required timing or contents.** No one is directed to commission or fund it, and the Academies are given no deadline, methodology, or safety standard, so the release mechanism may never become usable.

44. **Sec. 7(a) — “Acting on” the report is ambiguous.** The text does not say whether Congress must adopt the report’s conclusion, merely consider it, or make an independent finding, inviting disputes about whether a terminating resolution satisfies the condition.

45. **Sec. 7(a) — The joint-resolution mechanism is underspecified.** It supplies no resolution text, expedited procedures, committee deadlines, or definition of enactment; a mere congressional vote would not ordinarily have legal effect without bicameral passage and presentment.

46. **Sec. 7 — The two termination provisions fit awkwardly together.** Section 7(a) says the prohibition lasts until a safety finding, but section 7(b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless of whether Congress ever makes that finding.

47. **Sec. 7(b) — The sunset ends more than the prohibition.** It terminates the registry, reporting duties, enforcement provisions, and international-agreement provision along with section 3, potentially eliminating records and enforcement authority concerning earlier conduct unless savings rules apply.

48. **Sec. 8 — The delayed effective date creates an unregulated preparation window.** During the 180 days after enactment, companies could start training to invoke section 3(b), reorganize through foreign entities, or distribute hardware among facilities before any provision takes effect.

49. **Act-wide — No recordkeeping or compute-tracing duty applies to developers.** The government may need detailed logs to prove that a run crossed the threshold, but the bill requires reports only from registered large-facility operators and does not require model developers to preserve evidence.

50. **Act-wide — No appropriation or administrative implementation framework is provided.** The responsible departments receive no express funding, staffing authority, rulemaking mandate, technical standards process, or coordination mechanism, which could make enforcement slow and inconsistent.

51. **Act-wide — There is no severability clause.** Although courts often apply a presumption of severability, the bill does not state whether the remaining provisions should survive if a definition, exception, extraterritorial application, or termination mechanism is invalidated.
